findings.analytical_note: Parisian origins of the Republic and control of local armed force made the Convention vulnerable to popular coercion. The departmental-guard proposal confronted rival understandings of national unity and independence.

Personal animosity and suspicions of massacre, royal collaboration and dictatorship shaped debates. Votes on appeal and clemency became durable factional markers; martyr cult and club exclusions hardened divisions.

Deputies including radicals initially rejected controls as economically harmful. Montagnard support later acknowledged the need for Parisian backing; economic doctrine alone cannot explain the May reversal.

Army provisioning, blockade, colonial crisis and depreciation compounded price rises. Women’s forced sales and increased pillage expressed real grievances; the author doubts a prior plot despite politicians’ accusations.

Conscription ignited accumulated religious, political and distributive grievances against town authorities who benefited from land sales and exemption. Noble leadership followed peasant mobilization, qualifying aristocratic-conspiracy explanations.

reader_access_routes: Resistance to the Revolution: geographic overview
findings.analytical_note: Rendered Map 4 gives a visual overview of resistance and campaign routes across 1793–1799. Its caption is substantive; detailed geographic evidence is treated as map context and linked to narrated events, without inventing prose treatment from a map label.

Weak garrisons and bocage favored rapidly assembling local forces, while republicans required concentration. Rebel expansion culminated in failure at Nantes; local attachment later constrained operations beyond home territory.
Better republican garrisons suppressed open Breton revolt and enforced quotas, while resistance continued as guerrilla warfare. This differs from the initial territorial success of the Vendée armies.

Military panic encouraged emergency justice and provincial emissaries; attacks on Girondin presses and failed insurrection established the possibility of purging representatives through popular action.
The new committees and local surveillance structures extended emergency power. Committee of Public Safety membership and effectiveness developed in stages; Robespierre initially declined membership.
Girondin removal of immunity and prosecution backfired after Marat’s acquittal and triumphant return, encouraging further sectional pressure.

Commercial disruption united workers and merchants against a militant minority’s threats, disarmament and exactions. The city’s earlier radical reputation does not establish uniform popular support for Jacobin government.

Opposition to local Jacobin extremism spread among people who had accepted republic and regicide; local club rivalries and sectional organization distinguish these cases from straightforward royalism.

reader_access_routes: Food supply and maximum: local constraints
findings.analytical_note: Luxury-demand collapse, lost markets and army competition undermined the city’s economy and provisioning. Threatened intervention by troops precipitated the sections’ overthrow of the municipality.

Renewed property-holder resistance and absence of Montagnard deputies on mission altered the parliamentary balance. Investigation and arrests of agitators and threats against Paris pushed initially reluctant Montagnards toward coercion.

The first rising was divided and inadequately mobilized; the renewed Sunday action physically confined deputies and forced arrests. Distinguish demands of Varlet, Commune moderates and Montagnards instead of presenting a single plan.

The purge neither overthrew a Girondin government nor destroyed an organized party. Doyle contrasts principled intransigence with pragmatic accommodation and locates much effective government in emissaries already inclined toward the Mountain.
Sansculotte vengeance and Montagnard fear for the Convention itself were different motives. Reluctant sacrifice of colleagues aimed to break paralysis during war, not merely seize new power.

reader_access_routes: Friends of Liberty and National Club
findings.analytical_note: Commercial crisis and rivalry of local clubs framed Bordeaux’s response. Actual insurrection followed June’s purge, with calls for a rival convention and departmental army far exceeding practical mobilization.
Cities coordinated resistance unevenly; several frontier centers drew back from rebellion. Lyons’s execution of Chalier deepened the conflict beyond constitutional protest.

Workload, migrant labor and depreciating wages drew dockworkers toward notables. Reopened sections displaced Jacobins, established punitive justice and arrested deputies; revival of religion distinguishes Toulon from other southern revolts.

Regional solidarity with purged deputies and constitutional protest coexisted uneasily with royalist military and social support. Girondin republicanism disappointed some hosts; Wimpffen’s possible English pay remains uncertain.

Doyle rejects inflated claims that most departments revolted and the idea of deliberate republican breakup. Leaders chiefly wanted a tranquil propertied republic; conscription, forced loans, policing and price controls provoked broader support than wealth alone explains.

Reluctance to serve far from home crippled recruitment and operations. Nantes’s resistance to Vendéan attack reconciled it to the Convention despite Girondin sympathies, illustrating divisions among opponents.

The Convention’s reluctance to criminalize colleagues and its prompt restraint of sectional organizers contradict a picture of unified radical triumph. Proposed revolutionary armies were internal vigilante forces, distinct from military front armies.

The constitution deliberately won popular assent through direct annual elections, expanded rights and legislative control of executive power. Ratification and ceremonial promulgation did not produce implementation; wartime emergency justified indefinite suspension.
Popular concessions included access to property and outright uncompensated abolition of remaining feudal rights, with destruction of their documentary basis. These are distinct rural reforms.

reader_access_routes: Committee of Public Safety: July changes
findings.analytical_note: Persistent subsistence grievances survived constitutional concessions; Montagnards attacked independent radical challengers. Corday acted alone, while Marat’s death became a political resource and government shifted toward more determined emergency action.
